content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a comprehensive framework to investigate the circumstances surrounding perinatal deaths, including stillbirths and neonatal deaths, with the goal of identifying preventable factors and improving care. This framework includes the Making Every Baby Count: Audit and Review of Stillbirths and Neonatal Deaths guide, which provides tools such as the Stillbirth and Neonatal Death Case Review Form and the Births and Deaths Summary Form. These tools are designed to facilitate the classification of stillbirths and neonatal deaths as part of an audit and response process. The WHO has also introduced the ICD-PM (International Classification of Diseases for Perinatal Mortality), which builds upon the existing ICD-10 system. This classification system links perinatal deaths to maternal conditions and emphasizes the mother-baby dyad, enabling healthcare providers to identify areas requiring programmatic interventions to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. The ICD-PM simplifies the certification of perinatal deaths while providing public health workers and program officers with actionable insights to address the needs of both mother and baby simultaneously. The data collection forms used in this system are designed to streamline data entry and analysis. However, they can be expanded to include more specific causes and categories depending on the capacity and interest of the healthcare facility staff and the perinatal mortality audit team. The ICD-PM also incorporates the timing of perinatal deaths (antepartum, intrapartum, or neonatal) and links these to maternal conditions, ensuring a comprehensive approach to mortality classification. The ICD-PM system is modeled on the ICD-MM (Maternal Mortality) framework, making it familiar to users of the ICD-10 system. However, the new concepts of timing and mandatory linkage to maternal conditions require ongoing monitoring and further research to optimize its application. This system not only enhances the clarity of perinatal death certification but also supports targeted interventions to reduce preventable deaths and improve health outcomes globally.
